core.text: To show that the action in an infinitive happened *earlier*, Latin uses **the perfect infinitive (the 'to have done' form)**. Active: perfect stem + -isse, *dormīvisse* — to have slept. Passive: perfect participle + *esse*, *raptam esse* — to have been taken. You meet it mostly after verbs of saying and knowing: *dīcit tē dormīvisse* — he says that you slept. Latin name: *īnfīnītīvus perfectī*.
In *she says that he slept*, the sleeping came before the saying. Latin shows that time difference on the infinitive itself.
Active: perfect stem + -isse. Passive: participle (agreeing with its subject) + esse. Both mean 'earlier than the main verb'.

invented.en: Marcus says that he wrote the letter.

core.text: Plain **the infinitive (the 'to' form)** means 'at the same time': *dīcit Mārcum dormīre* — he says Marcus is sleeping. The -isse form pushes it back: *dīcit Mārcum dormīvisse* — he says Marcus slept (or has slept).

teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Tap the word in each sentence that reports something that had already happened.

teach.say: When you report what somebody said or thought, and the thing reported happened earlier, Latin uses **the perfect infinitive (the 'to have done' form)**: *Iūlius dīcit Mārcum vēnisse* — Julius says that Marcus came. English says 'that he came'; Latin says, word for word, 'him to have come'.

check.ask: Which word reports something that already happened?

teach.title: The active form: perfect stem + -isse
teach.say: Take the perfect stem — the third dictionary form with its *-ī* cut off — and add *-isse*. *lēgī* gives *lēgisse*, *fēcī* gives *fēcisse*, *fuī* gives *fuisse*. One ending covers every verb in the book, and it never changes, whoever is being talked about.

check.ask: Fill in the perfect active infinitive.

teach.title: The passive form: participle + esse
teach.say: For something done to somebody, use the perfect participle with *esse*: *scrīptam esse*, *captum esse*. The participle is an adjective again here, so it takes the ending of the word the sentence is about: *rosās carptās esse*, because the roses are what is being reported.

check.ask: Fill in the perfect passive infinitive.

teach.title: Now, or already?
teach.say: The plain infinitive and the perfect infinitive sit one syllable apart. *scrībere* is 'to write', going on now; *scrīpsisse* is 'to have written', already over. Both follow *dīcit* in the same way, so only the ending tells you when the reported thing happened.

check.ask: *iisse* — is the master going now, or has he already gone?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: The person the report is about goes into the object form — *Mārcum*, *puerōs*, or *sē* when it is the speaker himself — and the infinitive comes last, however long the clause grows. Read the object form as 'that he', and the infinitive as the verb of that little sentence.

check.ask: *laudō, laudāre, laudāvī, laudātum*. Report that the boys were praised.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 21) remember -isse as a squeezed *esse*, and note that in the accusative + infinitive the passive participle agrees with the accusative subject: *vīdī eās relictās esse* — I saw that they had been left. A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) uses the passive shape with active sense: *audīvimus tē profectum esse* — we heard you had set out.
Some perfect infinitives stand for a present because the verb has no present: *meminisse* (to remember), *nōvisse* (to know), *ōdisse* (to hate).
